title: Shannon Entropy: Measuring Uncertainty
hook: How many bits does it take to describe the outcome of a random experiment? Shannon's entropy gives the answer.

equation.caption: Entropy of a discrete probability distribution.

steps: \text{Maximum entropy for } n \text{ outcomes: } \log_2 n = {{maxH}} \text{ bits}

explorations.title: Certainty vs. Uncertainty
explorations.predict: What happens to entropy when one outcome is certain?
explorations.why: When p_i = 1 for one outcome, its contribution is -1 * log2(1) = 0, and all other p_i = 0 contribute 0 (since 0 log 0 = 0). So H = 0.

explorations.title: Uniform Distribution
explorations.predict: What is the entropy when all outcomes are equally likely?
explorations.why: For n equally likely outcomes, each p_i = 1/n, so H = -n * (1/n) * log2(1/n) = log2(n). For n=4, log2(4)=2.

self_tests.name: Entropy less than maximum for non-uniform

limitation: This interactive assumes a discrete, finite probability distribution with no memory or correlation between outcomes. Real-world sources often have dependencies or continuous distributions, which require different entropy measures.
misconception: Entropy is not a measure of disorder or randomness in a physical sense; it quantifies the average uncertainty or information content in bits for a given probability distribution.

claims.text: Entropy is defined as H = -\sum p_i \log_2 p_i.
For a certain outcome, entropy is zero.
For n equally likely outcomes, entropy is log2(n) bits.
Our toy model normalizes probabilities and treats 0 log 0 as 0.

outcomes.outcome: Compute entropy for a given discrete probability distribution.
Explain why certainty yields zero entropy.
Verify that four equally likely outcomes give 2 bits of entropy.
Handle zero probabilities correctly in entropy calculation.
